questions.stem: You are examining Helen Marchetti, 46, in general practice. She has a firm, tender left retroareolar lump and nipple retraction. With a chaperone present you have already inspected her with her arms by her sides and then raised. Which manoeuvre best tests whether the mass is fixed to pectoralis major?
options: Ask her to lean forward with her arms hanging so that the breasts fall away from the chest
Ask her to raise both arms above her head while you look for skin dimpling
Ask her to press her hands firmly on her hips, then check how freely the mass moves
Lie her back at 45° with her hand behind her head, then palpate the mass
questions.why: Pressing the hands into the hips makes pectoralis major contract. If the mass moves less once the muscle is tensed, it is fixed to the deep fascia or muscle, which is a feature of malignancy.
notes: Leaning forward helps show asymmetry or skin tethering, especially in large breasts, but it does not tense pectoralis to test for deep fixation.
Raising the arms brings out skin dimpling and nipple changes from tethering to the skin, not fixation to the underlying muscle.
This is the position for systematic palpation, because it spreads the breast tissue over the chest wall. It does not contract pectoralis to test for deep fixation.

questions.stem: Mrs Marchetti, 46, has a 5 mL left retroareolar abscess. Deep to it is an irregular, vascular solid mass (category 4), with 6 mm skin thickening and an axillary node with a 5 mm cortex. You phone the breast clinic. What is the most appropriate way to get a tissue diagnosis of the mass?
options: Ultrasound-guided core biopsy now, in the same visit as aspiration of the abscess
Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology of the solid mass
Repeat the ultrasound after 2 weeks of antibiotics, then biopsy if the mass persists
Send the aspirated pus for cytology, and biopsy only if malignant cells are seen
questions.why: A suspicious solid mass needs a core biopsy at presentation, not after the infection settles. Core biopsy gives tissue architecture and receptor status, and is preferred to FNA. Triple-test concordance is needed before the lump can be called benign.
notes: FNA gives cytology only, with no tissue architecture or receptor status, and is less reliable than core biopsy for a solid lesion.
Waiting delays the diagnosis of a possible cancer. Biopsy should happen now, not after the infection settles.
Pus cytology is insensitive and does not sample the solid mass, so a negative result would give false reassurance.

questions.stem: On examination Mrs Marchetti, 46, has early peau d'orange over the inner left breast. Her ultrasound shows 6 mm skin thickening. Inflammatory breast cancer is in the differential. Which mechanism best explains the peau d'orange appearance?
options: Tumour shortening Cooper's ligaments and pulling focal areas of skin inwards
Dermal lymphatic obstruction causing oedema, with the skin tethered at hair follicles
Cytokine-driven dermal vasodilation and hyperaemia caused by the bacterial infection
Compression of superficial veins by the mass, causing venous congestion of the skin
questions.why: Peau d'orange is dermal oedema from blocked lymphatics, classically from tumour emboli in the dermal lymphatics in inflammatory cancer. The skin swells around hair follicles and sweat ducts, which stay tethered, giving the pitted orange-peel look.
notes: Shortening of Cooper's ligaments causes focal skin dimpling or tethering, not the diffuse pitted oedema of peau d'orange.
Vasodilation explains the redness and warmth, but not the pitted, thickened skin of lymphoedema.
Venous obstruction causes dilated superficial veins, not pitted dermal oedema; lymphatic blockage is the key mechanism.

questions.stem: Mrs Marchetti, 46, has a suspicious left retroareolar mass that extends into the upper inner quadrant. Ultrasound shows a left axillary node with a 5 mm cortex, and the breast surgeon plans to sample it. Which group of nodes receives most of the lymph drained from the breast?
options: Internal thoracic (parasternal) nodes, which lie alongside the sternum
Supraclavicular nodes, reached through the deep cervical chain
Contralateral breast, reached directly from the subareolar plexus
Axillary nodes, with the anterior (pectoral) group usually first
questions.why: About 75% of the breast's lymph, including lymph from the subareolar plexus, drains to the ipsilateral axillary nodes, usually reaching the anterior (pectoral) group first. This is why the axilla is examined and imaged in every breast lump assessment.
notes: The internal thoracic nodes take a smaller share of lymph, mainly from the medial breast. They are not the main drainage route, even for medial tumours.
Supraclavicular nodes are usually reached only after the axillary or apical nodes, so they are a later site of spread, not the main drainage.
Lymph only crosses to the opposite breast in a small amount, usually when the normal channels are obstructed. It is not the main route.
